Chapter 6
Results
Chapter abstract. This chapter reports the measured wave, the calibrated in-silico
experiment, and the balanced evidence synthesis. It covers descriptives, reliability,
CFA, hypothesis results, the G0/G1 contrast, calibration, the Bayesian check, joint
sensitivity, topology and persona checks, component ablations, source ablation, an-
chor bootstrap, held-out prediction, a Gemini persona-agent pilot, and a human-gold
validation of machine qualitative coding.
It distinguishes measured, model-based,
and legacy stress-test ndings and reports frequentist and Bayesian summaries side
by side.
This chapter preserves reported questionnaire results, historical respondent-
level sensitivity, qualitative themes, and a joint display, separated from the histor-
ical calibrated simulation. The interpretation of Student Rating is separated from
episode evaluation and from the extended study design. Field tables and gures re-
produce the measured-wave exports included in the reproducibility archive; the nal
calibrated pipeline is reported separately in Section 6.12. The historical two-arm
simulation and its Bayesian summary retain the original study's model summaries;
their provenance is distinguished in Appendix L. A model contrast is not an observed
eld intervention eect.

The

composite of raw interaction. The measured PB and star ratings are the human an-

6.1
The Measured Wave
6.1.1
Sample Description
The analytic sample comprised 52 university students, 30 male and 22 female, fol-
lowing eight historical exclusions from 60 collected questionnaires. The retained-ID
list reproduces the sample; the precise duplicate key is examined in Section 6.4. The
setting was social media radio listening associated with Uber journeys in the 6th of
October City area, Giza. The export lists six institutional categories, with counts
of 12, 5, 13, 3, 13, and 6. These are sample categories, not estimates of institutional
populations. Reported ride duration ranged from 5 to 15 minutes. Interaction was
self-reported as minimal, low, moderate, or high.

6.1.3
Associations Among Audience Evaluations
PB was positively associated with the star rating (ρ = .671), reported interaction
(ρ = .601), and ride duration (ρ = .616). The broadcaster-rating subscales were
also positively associated with PB: BR, .809; SV, .952; and IQ, .946. Durationstar
correlation was .309. All coecients are Spearman correlations from the supplied
association export; they are not standardised regression coecients or causal eects.
The very high SVPB and IQPB associations raise an interpretive question.
They may reect shared audience evaluation, but they may also reect substan-
tive overlap and common response processes. A separate star-rating block provides
convergent self-report evidence, not an independent criterion of information accu-
racy or a demonstrated learning gain. The export stores the starPB probability as
zero at its output precision; an exact zero probability is not reported here, and no
unreported condence intervals are constructed from the summary alone.

6.4
Respondent-Level Recheck and Exclusion Sensitivity
The inherited audit describes a respondent-level reanalysis in addition to cross-le
summary checks. The les are absent from the present archive; the following is
a historical account, not a fresh rerun. The 52 retained identiers reproduce the
reported PB mean and SD, star mean, alpha coecients, PB item means and SDs,
and six principal Spearman associations to the displayed precision. BR4 is reversed
as 4 −BR4 before forming the four-item BR score.
There are no missing item
responses in the supplied 60-record questionnaire le.
The raw le contains 16 scale items and one star rating, not 21 scale items.
Removing exact duplicates on these 17 responses alone would exclude 34 records;
using all non-identier questionnaire elds would exclude four. Neither rule recon-
structs the historical eight exclusions. The newly supplied processing specication
identies a 21-eld key: the 16 scale responses, star rating, age, ride duration, traf-
c category, and interaction category. Applying exact equality on those elds to
the 60-record merged matrix and retaining the rst record reproduces exactly the
eight exclusions and the retained 52 cases. The retained item and context values
also agree with the earlier analysis matrix. Thus the earlier account species an
operational lter for future reproduction; its description must not call all 21 elds
scale items. This agreement does not establish when the rule was chosen, or that
matching responses necessarily identify the same person. The main analysis retains
the historical subset, reports all-60 sensitivity, and does not classify the excluded
participants as fraudulent.

6.5.1
T1: Accountable Practice and Social Endorsement
The accounts oer two dierent grounds for credibility. One concerns how claims
are handled: SR002 values transparent correction, SR009 values primary sources,
SR0017 values neutral moderation, and SR0033 values source acknowledgment. The

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
173
recorded remark for SR002 states: Transparency in admitting mistakes builds far
more credibility than pretending to be an infallible expert. These cases position
credibility as something a broadcaster demonstrates in communication, rather than
merely possesses as a reputation score.
Other cases locate trust in peer feedback and visible community ratings
(SR0012, SR0016, SR0025, SR0060). SR0012's recorded remark says, Peer reviews
make it easier to trust new broadcast hoststhis is how radio should build credi-
bility in the digital age.
This is a dierent mechanism: social endorsement can
guide judgment without establishing factual accuracy. T1 therefore complicates,
rather than validates, a single BRS construct. Neither the account claiming that di-
verse viewpoints prevent polarisation (SR0042) nor the account praising trac-note
accuracy (SR0056, T5) is a measurement of those claimed eects.
6.5.2
T2: Peer Voices and Socially Local Radio
Student voices are described as familiar, spontaneous, and socially proximate. SR001
contrasts unedited student speech with conventional morning shows; SR0026 and
SR0040 contrast conversational delivery with rehearsed radio. SR0011 connects fa-
miliar banter with feeling less isolated, while SR0036 connects peer audio notes with
solidarity during nals. These meanings suggest that voice and social identication
are part of evaluation, not incidental features of content delivery.
The interpretation remains situated. The archive does not establish sustained
changes in loneliness, campus belonging, or mental health. Nor does familiarity make
a source accurate. For EST, this theme identies a plausible audience-level pathway
that should not be absorbed into architecture alone: a student's prior connection to

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
174
the voices may shape the judgment of the same interface.
6.5.3
T3: A Worthwhile Ride Need Not Be an Interactive Ride
The most widely coded theme concerns the t between audio and the immediate
journey. Calm matters in accounts of fatigue and stress; brevity and clear structure
matter when listening time is limited.
SR003's recorded remark states, Audio
platforms should feel like a cozy lounge rather than an aggressive ad strip. SR0014
values short segments, and SR0031, SR0041, SR0046, SR0049, and SR0054 value
concise or clearly structured delivery. These are accounts of situated usefulness, not
measurements of learning gain.
The paired cases show why activity is an incomplete measure of value. SR003
has low recorded interaction but PB of 5.6; SR0011 also has low interaction with PB
of 5.0. Conversely, SR0018 appreciates the low-key tone while giving PB of 3.0 and
two stars. A favourable comment about one feature can coexist with an unfavourable
overall evaluation. This does not negate the positive pooled interactionPB associ-
ation; it prevents reading that association as a universal equation between visible
action and worthwhile listening.
6.5.4
T4: Agency, Contribution, and Protected Access
SR004's topic vote and SR0019's visible poll response are recorded instances of in-
uencing the communication process. Creator-oriented accounts are more tentative:
SR0013, SR0024, and SR0051 ask how to contribute or express an intention to do
so. Their enthusiasm is not evidence that a broadcast was subsequently produced,
independently veried, or used for learning.

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
175
Participation is also conditional on access and control. SR0034 values an
anonymous participation option, and SR0030 requests custom topic lters.
The
latter is a constructive criticism, not an observation that the feature already worked.
SR0059 oers technical feedback. Together these accounts position participation as
an opportunity to shape the platform, not simply a high interaction count. They
inform EST-P4's proposed aordances without establishing a causal benet of those
aordances.
6.5.5
T5: Relevance Grounded in Student-Lived Needs
Practical topics recur: student trade (SR001), side-hustle issues (SR005), remote
work (SR0038), graduate interviews (SR0044), trac (SR0056), and startup fund-
ing (SR0057). Campus updates and environmental participation appear in SR008
and SR0029. The recorded remark for SR0038 identies part-time remote work op-
portunities as the kind of practical content students need. Interest in a technology
discussion (SR0039) and an AI-ethics debate (SR0022) indicates that relevance is
not conned to immediate utility.
These cases supply a reason to build and compare topic repertoires. They
do not show that all members of a faculty share the same preferences. The supplied
proles repeatedly connect discipline to interests; using those connections as deter-
ministic agent rules would reproduce the archive's framing rather than test it. Topic
preference should be individually grounded and capable of changing with context.

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
176
6.5.6
T6: Delivery and Interface Quality as Enabling Conditions
Several accounts praise clarity, continuity, latency, or interface design.
SR006,
SR0021, SR0047, SR0050, and SR0058 describe audio delivery; SR0027 values visual
simplicity, and SR0052 values one-tap controls. SR0037 states a conditional prefer-
ence: As long as the audio doesn't cut out and the content isn't annoying, I prefer
social radio over static FM noise. This is a threshold of acceptability rather than
evidence that more interaction or more technical sophistication is always better.
Engineering-sounding remarks remain experiential reports. No buer trace,
latency benchmark, security audit, or packet-loss test follows merely from a rider
describing a stream as robust. Equally, a transcript-only LLM cannot reproduce an
audio-quality judgment simply by being told that the stream is excellent. Technical
telemetry and listening modality must be separated in the planned agent extension.
6.5.7
Tensions, Additional Cases, and Evidential Limits
The eight records outside the historical quantitative subset add two T3, two T4,
three T5, and one T6 memberships. They do not introduce a seventh theme under
this codebook, but that observation is not a saturation claim. Their continued inclu-
sion prevents a numeric ltering decision from silently removing distinct qualitative
accounts.
The corpus is overwhelmingly favourable. Its main qualifying cases concern
quiet appreciation, conditional preference, and suggested improvements rather than
sustained rejection.
This imbalance may reect selection, the recording process,
or the social circumstances of the encounter; the present archive cannot separate

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
177
these explanations. The analysis preserves that limitation instead of construing the
absence of extensive criticism as unanimous support.
6.6

pretation that audience evaluation combines content, social cues, reception condi-
tions, and interface experience. It does not transform a cross-sectional association
into an architectural eect.

6.7
Focus-Group Synthesis: Prototype Participation and De-
sign
The FGD contributes four provisional domains without enlarging the questionnaire
or rider-record denominators. These are ndings of the narrative synthesis dened in
Section 5.4, not newly authenticated participant quotations. Appendix G preserves
the full account and verication boundaries.
FGD-T1: Listening, practice, and publication. One reported account
describes recording privately for self-training and discarding recordings rather than
publishing. Private practice may be the intended activity, not failed participation
or evidence of anxiety. The label Podcast Paradox remains an analytical shorthand,
not a validated construct.
FGD-T2: Collaboration and choice. Co-hosting is presented through
a peer-conversation and radio call-in rationale. Favourable reactions are reported
without attributable extracts or subsequent publishing behaviour.
Optional and
mandatory co-hosting remain competing choices: an unavailable peer could con-
strain rather than enable an otherwise willing participant.
FGD-T3: Institutional access and visibility. The described ID/PIN
arrangement places the proposed service in an ACU context and raises questions
about eligibility, privacy, and identiable speech. Membership restrictions do not
demonstrate safety, condentiality, or psychometric validity. This FGD does not
test EST-P3.
FGD-T4: Interface cues and idle content. Proles, timestamps, Boost

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
179
invitations, and fallback music or advertising identify possible coordination mecha-
nisms. Screen interaction alone does not demonstrate comprehension, usability, or
improved evidence-based production.
6.7.1
Supplemental Review Without Evidence Promotion
The subsequently supplied seven-part generated analysis does not establish new par-
ticipant ndings. Its suggestions about long-programme preferences and registration
feedback are retained as questions within FGD-T1 and FGD-T4, not conrmed ex-
periences or additional themes. Inconsistent translations, unknown speaker roles,
and invalid timestamp strings prevent adoption of its bilingual passages as verbatim
evidence. Statements of consensus, improved retention, reduced anxiety, safety, or
resolved production barriers are not accepted as outcomes. The four domains re-
tain their provisional status; Appendix G.4 distinguishes retained review leads from
claims withheld or rejected.
6.7.2
Integration with the Rider Accounts
The sources complement one another at the level of questions, not linked cases. The
FGD's distinction between listening and publishing resonates with rider accounts
of quiet appreciation; collaboration complements accounts of socially local radio;
access conditions and interface choices elaborate participatory agency and delivery.
These similarities neither merge the codebooks nor prove independent corrobora-
tion: source provenance and participant overlap remain unresolved. No FGD theme
receives a rider PB score or enters the rider case-coverage chart.
The integrated interpretation is that listening, private practice, co-hosting,

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
180
and public publishing may represent dierent goals rather than successive levels of
engagement. This motivates competing simulation mechanisms (Section 5.9), not
numerical parameters or conrmation of H1H7. The reported duration is compat-
ible with approximately 28 minutes, but a visual timestamp at 30:30 remains in-
consistent under a shared time origin. Technical audio gures and unaudited word
counts therefore receive no quantitative calibration weight.
The new rule-based
comparator and LLM-agent extension remain unexecuted.
6.8
Interpretation of Student Rating Impact
The empirical evidence concerns students' evaluations of social media radio and the
meanings recorded in their accounts. PB is a multi-item experience measure, and
its association with stars is convergent audience evidence.
Neither measure is a
substitute for the Student Rating competence prole in Section 3.7. The survey
contains no NMLS item responses or paired competence assessments; consequently
no Student Rating treatment eect is estimated from these 52 records.
The qualitative analysis nevertheless identies mechanisms relevant to SR:
source appraisal and correction in T1, participation conditions in T4, and student-
relevant production interests in T5. These are reasons to examine competence and
opportunity directly, not evidence that every participant acquired the corresponding
skill. Statements of willingness to create are also distinct from completed, indepen-
dently assessed media artifacts.
The historical model's +.165 star dierence and +.511 PB dierence retain
their original interpretation as modelled broadcast evaluations. They are not rela-

CHAPTER 6. RESULTS
181
belled as literacy gains, higher Student Rating, or attainment of a level of demon-
strated human competence. The next extension uses independent task accuracy as
its primary computational outcome and the full NMLS prole only as a secondary
synthetic diagnostic. It tests conditional platform eects, not human student devel-
opment. Its estimands are specied in Section 5.10.12; no future run is included in
the reported results.
No synthetic pilot-consensus result is included: its raw traces and claimed
validation outputs are absent from this archive. A condence proxy cannot establish
a measured competence threshold or validate EST.
6.9
Hypothesis Results
The H1H7 identiers are retained; H7 now species the prospective computational
task test rather than a retrospectively measured eld outcome.
Evaluation dis-
tinguishes observed associations, conditional simulation contrasts, and direct tests
of the specied outcomes. A positive association is not a causal nding, and the
absence of a suitable test is not conrmation.
6.9.1
H1: Structural Credibility (EST-P1)
The measured starPB association shows agreement between forms of audience eval-
uation. The model reports ∆PB = +.511 and a star-rating dierence of +.165 under
G1 relative to G0. These ndings are consistent with H1's direction, but do not iso-
late a causal eect of displayed BRS in the eld sample.

What the Final Experiment Shows
The calibrated in-silico experiment shows what the specied design implies. First,
the assumed state-outcome weights produce a clear, internally coherent contrast in
both evaluative and competence-format Student Ratings. Second, that contrast is
accompanied by an assumed engagement cost, which is the central trade-o the
thesis argues for. Third, the 256-point joint sweep shows how the contrast depends
on six mechanism parameters and ve state-outcome weights; its sign and magnitude
are not independent of those assumptions. Fourth, the main simulator gives similar
signs across three graph generators, and the persona-prior variants remain positive.
